Opoczno New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Opoczno, Poland

Demolished. Opoczno, founded at the turn of the 13th-14th centuries under Środa law, recorded Jews from 1501; an 1646 permit authorized both a synagogue and cemetery. Population grew from 42.7% (477) in 1790 to 57.1% (1,703) by 1863, with Opoczno becoming a prominent Hasidic center; by 1937, 3,400 Jews lived there. A late-1940 ghetto's October 27, 1942 liquidation deported nearly 3,000 to Treblinka (200 dying during the process); the remaining 500 were sent via a temporary camp in Ujazd before also reaching Treblinka. This newer cemetery, established in 1829 and closed by the late 1930s, was reopened during WWII after Germans forbade use of the older cemetery outside town limits, and held execution-victim mass graves. In 1945, three exhumed bodies from Trojanowice plus a Jewish Polish Army officer were reburied here - likely the site's final burials. Post-1949 looting stripped matzevot and wall fragments for construction material; a 1960s park replaced the ruined grounds, with 1976-1980 rainwater drainage construction further disturbing the site. Surviving tombstone fragments are held at the Opoczno Regional Museum.
